claims.text: Equiatomic high-entropy solid-solution nanoparticles inherently exhibit severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion raises atomic diffusion barriers.
Severe lattice distortion raises the energy barrier for defect clustering.
Severe lattice distortion promotes rapid interstitial-vacancy recombination.
Enhanced interstitial-vacancy recombination inhibits the initiation of phase separation and precipitation.
High-entropy solid solutions can remain single phase during elevated-temperature exposure.
The proposed nanoparticles will remain stable without phase separation or precipitation throughout 473–1923 K.
The initial nanoparticles comprise at least five metals in near-equal atomic ratios and have a single solid-solution phase with uniform elemental distribution.
Using an inert atmosphere ensures that thermal energy is the only driving force acting on the nanoparticles.
High-lattice-distortion nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous single-phase solid solution up to 1923 K.
High-lattice-distortion nanoparticles will undergo minimal grain coarsening up to 1923 K.
A slightly off-equiatomic composition can be designed to have less lattice distortion than the equiatomic composition.
Nanoparticles with reduced lattice distortion will develop detectable phase separation or precipitation at lower temperatures than high-distortion nanoparticles.
Above about 1923 K or in reactive environments, additional thermally activated processes may affect stability.
Processing or heating rates may change the temperature at which distortion-induced suppression of diffusion is overcome.
Comparable or greater phase separation, precipitation, or grain growth in the high-distortion sample than in the reduced-distortion control within 473–1923 K would falsify the hypothesis.
